utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-R77.4, the Prosecutor versus Astrit Haraqija and Bajrush Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Morina, can you hear me in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED MORINA: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, can you hear me -- THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in a language you understand? I think you said yes already before I finished my question, but apparently no problem there. May I have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Daniel Saxon for the Prosecution, together with our case manager, Mr. Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. For the Defence, Haraqija Defence first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If it please Your Honours, good morning. Karim Khan for the respondent, Astrit Haraqija, assisted by my learned friend pro bono legal assistant Caroline Buisman on my right and on the far right legal assistant Gissou Azarnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. And for Mr. Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jens Dieckmann, Defence counsel for Mr. Bajrush Morina, and on the left side IS our legal assistant Ms. Christine Kerll and pro bono assistant Danielle Paten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They're all a bit hidden behind screens, but thank you, Mr. Khan. Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann. We are here for the trial today of Mr. Morina and Mr. Haraqija. Mr. Morina is charged with contempt. Mr. Haraqija is charged with contempt and incitement to contempt. Mr. Saxon, and I'm also addressing the Defence, I do understand that you'd like to make a short opening statement, and that the Defence refrains at least at this moment from making an opening statement and it's still open whether an opening statement would be made at the beginning of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's quite correct. There won't be an opening statement; however, I did indicate before court that Mr. Haraqija intends to avail himself under Rule 84 bis of making a sworn statement from the dock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 84 bis, is that a sworn statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused can't be compelled, as I understand it, to give a sworn statement, but it's a matter of Your Honours' discretion. The reason, in all candour, of why I am of the mind and the accused is minded to give a sworn statement is two-fold. Firstly, it may incrementally increase the weight of what he says because it's sworn and the consequences of perjury. Secondly, we keep open the possibility as I alerted my learned friend for the Prosecution before the weekend that Mr. Haraqija may elect to give evidence in his own defence. Should that be the case, it will be a short matter, but it will save us having to go over all the issues that he mentions in his unsworn statement, and it allows the Prosecution to cross-examine him quite properly on matters that are raised now. So I think it's also a function of -- well, it also has the advantage, in my respectful submission, of some judicial economy. So those are the two reasons why I would urge that the statement be sworn. It won't be very long, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, what's your position as far as giving a sworn statement under Rule 84 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no objection as long as obviously the Prosecution then would have an opportunity to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say the short statement under Rule 84 bis would then trigger a right to cross-examine Mr. Haraqija; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, because Rule 84 bis, Your Honour, does not require a solemn declaration - but my learned friend is suggesting that we use that procedure now - it seems to me, then, the Prosecution should have the opportunity to test the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I do understand you do consider it to be evidence because at the same time, Mr. Khan, I hear you say that Mr. Haraqija may decide to take the stand as a witness in his own case, but that you consider a statement under Rule 84 bis not to trigger the right to cross-examine the accused on his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour is quite right that as a matter of construction, 84 bis is an opportunity for an accused to give a statement and there's no right of cross-examination from that. The rule, of course, is permissive in nature in my submission. He can't be compelled to make a sworn statement; but Your Honours in your inherent discretion may allow him to give a sworn statement should he wish to do so. Your Honours, at the end of the proceedings, you will decide after hearing all the evidence what weight, if any, to accord to this unsworn statement, as you will in relation to all the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: My simple point is if it is sworn and if the accused does elect to give evidence, it obviates the need to rehash any matters that have been raised by the accused now. If he doesn't elect to give evidence, of course, Your Honours will decide what weight is appropriate at the end of the trial. It was an attempt to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there is no doubt about that. Mr. Khan, is there any precedent of accused giving sworn statements under Rule 84 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not aware of any. The cases I'm aware of where accused have given statements from the dock, they have been unsworn. Your Honour, I'm in your hands. It's not a matter I'm urging you very strongly one way or the other, but I don't see any harm in the proposal that I put forward; but, of course, I'm in your hands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has briefly considered the matter. If the accused chooses to make a sworn statement to which he cannot be compelled under Rule 84 bis, then the Chamber rules that the Prosecution is entitled to cross-examine the witness on that statement. The Chamber does appreciate that you have tried to assist us in judicial economy, Mr. Khan. It's not without reason that I ask you whether there was any precedent because I was not aware of it. So it's new territory, so to say, but this is the ruling of the Chamber. If Mr. Haraqija chooses to give the solemn declaration at the beginning of his statement, then the Prosecution will have an opportunity to cross-examine him, still to be considered at what time exactly because that raises another matter; that is, whether or not an accused taking the stand should be examined first as what I understand is at least a tradition in English law, not in all the systems, but at least in English law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful. I didn't intend at all to complicate matters. I think the simplest thing in that case is the accused can be invited to give an unsworn statement from the dock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If I call the accused, I will indicate now and I did indicate to my learned friend as well; and, indeed, it was the Prosecution's suggestion to which I readily agreed that he will be my first witness before I call any other witnesses in the Defence case. And, of course, it's open to the Prosecution even without the evidence being under oath that they have leave, with Your Honour's consent of course, to cross-examine on any matters, including anything he may say in the dock at the moment. So, Your Honours, perhaps he can be invited in due course to give an unsworn statement from the dock; it may be simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Having settled this matter, Mr. Saxon, are you ready to give your, as I understand, brief opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I hope it will be brief, Your Honours. Just one question, the Prosecution has two, hopefully, brief administrative matters to raise. Would the Chamber like me to raise them before my opening statement or after?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they affect the opening statement, you're invited to do it before the opening statement; if not, let's start with the opening statement so that at least we know what your case is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I will proceed with the opening statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this case is about a deliberate and calculated effort by Astrit Haraqija and Bajrush Morina to interfere with a protected witness in a trial before this Tribunal. At the time of these events, July 2007, Astrit Haraqija was the minister for culture, youth, and sport in Kosovo. Bajrush Morina, a journalist by background, was employed in the same ministry as a political adviser to Angelina Krasniqi, one of the deputy ministers. Morina had interviewed the protected witness for a newspaper article several years earlier. In early July 2007, Haraqija instructed Morina to contact the protected witness in his country of residence and arrange for Morina and Haraqija to travel to that country in order to speak directly with the protected witness. The purpose of the visit was to convince the protected witness to change or withdraw his testimony against Ramush Haradinaj in case number IT-04-84. And you will find evidence of this, Your Honours, in Exhibits 1 and 2, recordings of the conversations that took place; and Exhibits 3 and 4, the ICTY statements of the protected witness; as well as Exhibit 8, the OTP's suspect interview with Mr. Morina. Initially, both Haraqija and Morina intended to travel to meet the protected witness, and you'll find evidence of this in Exhibit 8; Exhibit 11, which are travel documents obtained from the Kosovo Ministry of Youth, Culture, and Sport; and Exhibit 12, a series of SMS messages sent by Morina to the cellular telephone of the protected witness before their first meeting. Since Morina knew the protected witness but Haraqija did not, Morina's role, initially, was to introduce Morina to the protected witness. Morina would speak with the protected witness on 10 July, and then Haraqija would meet with the protected witness on 11 July, after Morina had explained to the witness the nature of the -- the reasons why they were coming to see him. However, Mr. Haraqija eventually decided not to travel to the third country and meet with the protected witness directly. Mr. Haraqija directed Mr. Morina to meet with the protected witness and tell him that the protected witness was one of three persons who could save Ramush Haradinaj, and to try to convince the protected witness to change or withdraw his testimony. Haraqija told Mr. Morina, his subordinate: "Go, or it won't be good for you." You'll find that at Exhibit 1A, page 24. On Saturday, the 10th of July, Mr. Morina met with the protected witness in a hotel. Mr. Morina followed the instructions of his minister, Mr. Haraqija, but the protected witness refused to change his plans to testify before this Tribunal. Mr. Morina was not aware at that time that, in order to protect the witness's safety and security, the meeting was being recorded by a witness protection unit of the police force in the country where the protected witness resides. And you'll find that in Exhibits 1, 3, and 4 -- 1, 2, 3, and 4, I should say. After that initial conversation, Mr. Morina attempted to inform Mr. Haraqija about the results of the meeting; however, Mr. Morina was not able to reach Mr. Morina [sic]; and, instead, Mr. Morina provided the information to Veli Bytyqi, the minister's spokesperson. On Sunday, the 11th July, Mr. Morina and the protected witness met again in a hotel and discussed the same issues. Again, you'll see that in Exhibits 2, 3, and 4. The protected witness stuck to his position that he would not change his testimony. During this trial, you will receive evidence demonstrating that Mr. Haraqija served as the deputy chairman of the "Defence Committee for Ramush Haradinaj," a committee established to raise funds to pay the costs of Mr. Haradinaj's defence. And there are documents pertaining to this committee in Exhibit 16. Mr. Haraqija believed that by prosecuting Mr. Haradinaj for the events that occurred in Kosovo in 1998, for certain events, this Tribunal was equating Kosovo Albanian victims with their executioners. You'll find that, Your Honours, in Exhibit 9, pages 12 and 13, the OTP's suspect interview with Mr. Haraqija conducted on 27 October 2007. Your Honours, pursuant to Rule 77(A)(iv) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Mr. Haraqija and Mr. Morina committed contempt of the Tribunal by interfering with a witness who was about to give evidence in proceedings before a Chamber. Mr. Haraqija's guilt is not diminished by the fact that he sent Mr. Morina as a messenger to deliver this message. Indeed, this conduct by a person in Mr. Haraqija's position of authority aggravates Mr. Haraqija's level of criminal responsibility. The actions of Mr. Haraqija also amount to the alternative crime of inciting contempt of the Tribunal, as prohibited by Rule 77(B). In the Beqaj judgement, the Trial Chamber noted that: "Incitement is defined in common-law systems as encouraging or persuading another to commit an offence, and one line of authority would also view threats or other forms of pressure as a form of incitement. Civil-law systems punish direct and public incitement assuming the form of provocation which is defined as an act intended to directly provoke another to commit a crime or a misdemeanour." In this case, Mr. Haraqija incited Mr. Morina to commit content of this Tribunal by directing, encouraging, persuading, or pressuring Mr. Morina to travel to meet the witness to deliver a message intended to dissuade the witness from testifying. Your Honours, the evidence that you will hear during this trial will convince you beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Morina and Mr. Haraqija are guilty as charged. That concludes the Prosecution's opening statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Haraqija --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Khan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I was addressing Mr. Haraqija because Mr. Khan already announced that Mr. Haraqija would like to make a statement under Rule 84 bis. Mr. Haraqija, you have an opportunity to do so. Your statement is given under the control of this Trial Chamber, and we'll carefully consider whether your statement is pertinent to this case. THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would also like to inform you that whatever you say, the Chamber may consider it to see whether and what probative value it has. So it could - of course, I do not know what the content is - it could be used against or, of course, in favour of you. Could you tell us approximately how much time you would need for this statement? THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] I would say ten minutes max.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you may proceed, Mr. Haraqija. THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must admit that I'm quite offended to be here on the desk of the accused. A good name to be blemished by an international indictment and to face an accusation. I cannot call it anything else but a trauma experience. This is the situation I find myself in today. The Kosovar society is complex and has many nuances. I will not go into details, but I find myself divided into two. I'm in the fight against the accusations of the Prosecution which is not true, and nothing will change that reality. My wife was a witness and she was present when I was accused of crimes against the Tribunal. There was no such discussion on my part as the Prosecution says. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] My microphone is switched on, but now you hear me again. If I may give you some guidance. Your plea of not guilty is on the record so that your challenge the charges brought against you is clear and doesn't need any repetition at this moment. At the same time, until now we have not heard things that are assisting the Chamber and are very pertinent to this trial. So if you please focus on matters pertinent and relevant for us to hear at this moment, that would be appreciated. Please proceed. THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my lawyer advised me to tell you a word or two about myself. As you know, my name is Astrit Haraqija, born in 1972, 14th June, in Gjakova municipality with an Asian tradition. I got married after the war, the 1999 war. I have two children, an 8-year-old boy Klesta, and a daughter who will be four years old in five days. In 1994, I started -- I involved myself in policy -- in politics, sorry. After six months, I was nominated as the leader of the Democratic Legal Alliance branch in Gjakova. I started my activities as the leader of the youth organization, the only one functioning in the Gjakova municipality at the time, because all the students and teachers were expelled from schools. It was mainly our organization led by me that dealt with the cultural and sport activities and organized this life in the Gjakova municipality, trying to support the Albanian population at the time when the Serb services started to threaten the activists of human rights in Kosova. During this occupation I, as I said, dealt with the youth forum and dealt with cultural and sports activities till 1999. In 1997, I had my initial contacts with the KLA, in the end of this year. From this time on, I had mainly contacts concerning food and clothes. In 1998, in November, I was proclaimed terrorist by the Serb authorities. From this moment on, I lived in illegality; and until the war ended, I stayed in the mountains together with other people who had links with the KLA. Gjakova was liberated on the 14th June 1999, which coincides with my birthday. Afterwards, I started to deal with the organization of the institutional life in the municipality of Gjakova. I opened the office of the LDK in Gjakova, the branch in Gjakova; and the following day, we organized a press conference by Edita Tahiri, Lutfi Havazi, Haliz Gagica. In this press conference, it was said that the LDK exists and that the president is alive and feeling well, and that he would be coming back to Kosova soon. Soon afterwards, I became the opposition of the local self-government in our municipality. The headquarters had nominated this authority; and at the same time, they requested me to become the mayor of the Gjakova municipality. I refused this post because I did not support the standpoints of the KLA at that time. For the first time, I met with the now late-President Rugova in 1994 who was the chairman of the LDK in Kosova. Until 1999, I mainly dealt with Fehmi Agani, Bardhyl Caushi, both of them late, and the president of the branch, Mr. Shehu. After the NATO air campaign in 1999, I began my direct contacts with the late-President Rugova, since a small number of people continued to support the ideas of Rugova even in 1999. I became very close with Mr. Rugova and I liked his ideas; I found them phenomenal and I defended them. He had a very great influence in my life, and he was an inspiration for me. He continues to inspire me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you to have a pause because the French translation was a bit behind. You may proceed. THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As I said, he deeply influenced my life, my existence, and he inspired me. He continues to inspire me even from his grave. He's an individual who didn't talk much, who would never tell someone to shut up or order someone to leave his office. In general, he was very calm and peaceful person, although he grew up only with his mother, without with his father who had been killed by the Serb authorities, both his father and his grandfather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, it seems that you're now going into details on matters which are not of primary relevance for the case. Please proceed. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I hear what Your Honour's saying; and, of course, the accused, in my respectful submission -- the respondent, in my respectful submission, has indicated he'll be rather brief. He's going to be ten or 15 minutes at most. The matters, again in my respectful submission, are relevant. He's talking about his relationship with the LDK, and the Prosecution have made it very clear in their pre-trial brief that they ascribe a motive to my client, to Haradinaj, who's, of course, of a completely different party. So the links to the LDK and the lack of evidence and the lack of a link to the AAK goes to one of the relevant issues in my case. Your Honour, the other matters, of course, regarding his functions in Kosovo are generally relevant to propensity and sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, I stopped the witness when he started to go into the details about the personality of a person he said inspired him politically, and that is why I intervened. Please proceed, Mr. Haraqija, and please keep in mind what I just said. THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my ties were with Mr. Rugova since I was given the right upon counselling my lawyer to speak about Astrit Haraqija; but if you decide the opposite, I can stop now. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you have to stop. Of course, if you give us an impression of your person by explaining what you did, you're free to do so; but when you started telling us about the qualities and the personality of Mr. Rugova, I considered that to be not relevant for this case. Of course, your political orientation and affiliation has some relevance for this case; but please, without going into details, tell about yourself and not about the people who primarily inspired you in political terms. Please proceed. THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] All right. I would again stress that I'm happy to be -- to have been at the service of Mr. Rugova, and thanks to him now we have freedom in Kosova and in our state.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the year. THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] In cooperation with the organization, Elita, functioning in Gjakova municipality, we opened this call for the minorities for the Roma, Ashkali, and the Egyptian minority, because at the time the situation was not very good. And in very difficult economic situation, people refused to go to school. The school founded by us offered a six-month curricula for the minority children before they started going to public schools. At the same year, the local elections were held. The LDK won --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, the interpreters, a few lines ago, did not hear in which year this took place; and since you now say "at the same year," could you please repeat what year you have in mind. THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] In 1999, we opened the offices of the LDK in Gjakova and in Pristina, so I refer to the same year when we opened the minority school. In 2000, the local elections were held and the LDK of Kosova won the elections at all levels, in all municipalities. The LDK, after the victory, proposed me to take up the office of the director for youth, culture, and sports in the municipality of Gjakova. I refused this offer because my aim, primary aim, was for the LDK to win the election, both the LDK and President Rugova. I had no other ambition or aim in mind. This was my only mission, to defend the president and his ideas and the ideas of the LDK party. I continued to work in this respect because at the time different individuals took us for collaborators with the authorities, Serb authorities, in Belgrade. Since I was a close person and very familiar with the ideas of President Rugova, it was my duty to explain to the inhabitants of Gjakova Municipality, over 50.000 - and we know each other very well - I felt it was my duty to explain to them that the allegations against Rugova and the LDK were not true. In 2003, I took up the duty of the president of the local self-government of Gjakova. This job was not very ordinary because the communist tradition that dominated for 50 years was still there. It wasn't usual for a young man wearing an earring to be the chairman of this body and to be the representative of the system; but on the other side, my name was known to all Gjakova public opinion because it had been there for the last nine years. During the 21 months of me being on this post, I made investments in Gjakova municipality above 22 million euros - and the budget was only 800 million -- 800.000 euros - thanks to the cooperation with the Italian KFOR in Gjakova who helped us with the infrastructure, the US aid, the American US aid, and the English organization as well as other organizations, NGOs from Sweden and Italy. In addition to the investments that I procured at that time, the UNMIK had put a condition for all these standards to be fulfilled. There was six standards, and I was supposed to report every six months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, you've used until now 15 minutes. You're going into details about the financing of your work, which does not assist the Chamber. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful. I know Your Honour is trying to be helpful. Of course, Mr. Haraqija is not a lawyer, but it's quite clear what he's trying to do is to show the investments he made and the assistance he gave to minorities in his municipality. That is, in my respectful submission, quite clearly relevant. There's no separate sentencing stage in the event that you are not -- in the event that you're persuaded by the Prosecution's case. Your Honour, the other aspect is, I do think his time spent may not have been perfect. It's a skill, of course, to know to be able assess reasonable time. But I do think we will finish this case tomorrow, including the Defence case and closing speeches. So I would ask Your Honours to be a little bit indulgent with the accused and allow him to carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, of course, has held positions which allow him to understand and to, I would say, control speeches. I stopped him again here when he went into details which are not assisting the Chamber. I did not want to stop him on the subject necessarily but on the details, especially where he indicated that he would need ten minutes and where until now he has used 15 minutes. Mr. Haraqija, would you please proceed and keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to belabour the point, and this is a matter perhaps I can raise in closing. I think the only point he was trying, to make to clarify, is he didn't pay all this himself, he didn't do it himself. He did it with the assistance of the international community. He was simply facilitating in whatever role he had; but, of course, it's the international community that takes a great deal of credit for this rebuilding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, anything else you would like to add where Mr. Khan has -- well, has interpreted what you intended to say? Is there anything else? THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I sincerely apologise. I respect the interpreters, and due to the interpretation I try to speak in short. I know that the points I've outlined require more than ten or 15 minutes; but if you deem that I should stop here, then I will stop, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't say that. Again, I suggested that you take the next two minutes to conclude your unsworn statement, so if you'd use those two minutes to tell us what you find most relevant. Please proceed. THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA: [Interpretation] Thank you. I mentioned the pre-status standards, six standards, and for the sole reason because these standards included freedom of movement, security, the Kosova Protection Corps, and so on and so forth. With the cooperation with the general at the time, we drafted the plan, we visited the camps. We invited them to come and visit us to see how the situation was in our municipality, to visit these minorities and to see that the security was at a high level, and they could come back to live in Gjakova. We had the same contacts with the Serb minority. As the chairman of the government, we worked and made efforts for these refugees to come back. In 2004, there was a central government in Kosova. As member of the leadership of the LDK, I did not agree with this idea for all the parties to lead Kosova because someone had to take up the responsibility, and my idea was for opposition and position. So with President Rugova and Fatmir Rexhepi, we persuaded the government for this idea. All the local offices opposed this idea because they wanted to have their representatives in the authorities. Why we did this? As I said, for someone to be held responsible. At that time, our idea won; and after that, I was offered the post of the minister of transport, and then I did not offer this -- I did not accept this post. Later on, I accepted the post of the minister of culture, sport, and youth. Why? In 2004, in Kosova there was a very difficult situation in Kosova as far as cultural heritage was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haraqija, I invited you to focus on matters most relevant for this Chamber, and I gave you two more minutes. You've taken now four, 30 seconds to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, as the Rules say, and as I explained to Mr. Haraqija, the statement is given under the control of the Chamber. I'm exercising this control at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and not starting a major debate on everything I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No, of course. Your Honour, it is a matter for you and your colleagues, and it's a matter of discretion. Simply, I want to say a few words which I hope will assist you in exercising that discretion. Your Honour, it is not needed, in my respectful submission, to guillotine these proceedings. The whole week has been set aside. The matters are relevant in our submission. We will be finished, including the Defence case, by tomorrow. The accused has said he is a young man. I know Your Honour has indicated he's an experience public speaker, but his own words are that this is a nerve-racking experience to be hauled from Kosovo to an international courts, and I would ask that a bit of compassion and understanding are shown. These are relevant matters. He is talking about his appointment, just now, to the minister of culture. It is in that capacity that the Prosecution bring this case in very large measure. So I would ask Your Honours to be a little bit more understanding for the accused. Your Honours, if you think otherwise, of course I will say no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unanimously, the Chamber considers that the subject of this statement under Rule 84 bis is such that no further time should be given to Mr. Haraqija to continue. Mr. Khan, of course, if there are matters which you consider of such importance, of course, you can call Mr. Haraqija to the stand to put further questions to him in relation to his --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- political background and his career. Thank you, Mr. Haraqija. Mr. Dieckmann, have I properly understood that Mr. Morina is not seeking to make a statement under Rule 84 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this understanding is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Saxon, you had two administrative matters. I take it you want to deal with them before you call your first witness. Now, the Chamber is aware that there is an issue about the first witness you would like to call, especially in terms of that he doesn't seek any protection; at the same time, that it might be wise to hear small portions of his evidence in private session because it's not the protection of this witness but it's rather the protection of the protected witness in the Haradinaj case which requires such a cautious approach. That is one of the issues the Chamber is aware of. The Chamber is aware of the exchange of views of the parties in respect of this. I don't know whether this was one of your subjects; but if so, then, the Chamber has decided that in private session the details such as where the witness lives and what his name is could be dealt with not in a public setting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. With all due respect, I recently received an e-mail suggesting that perhaps a motion should be made for a pseudonym, but I'm perfectly willing to do what the Chamber directs me to do, perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, we have further considered the matter now with the Registry; and for administrative technical reasons, I do understand that if we want to conceal the identity of the witness from the public - and that is, of course, not because we want to protect this witness, but mainly because the identity of this witness could reveal the identity of the protected witness who is relatively central in this case - that for those reasons we would need a pseudonym. Now, if you would make an oral application at this moment, and you may refer to the reasons I've just given, that goes quicker I think for an oral application for pseudonym for the witness, then, of course, we'll hear from the Defence whether there's any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the points that Your Honour has just made in the past few moments, the Prosecution would make a motion under Rule 75(A) to permit the first witness to testify with the use of a pseudonym. That would be the only protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the motion is granted, and the first witness you will call will testify under the pseudonym "Witness 1." Whenever the parties during the examination want to refer to events that might be central to his testimony, they are invited to refer to the country of residence rather than to name the country of residence of Witness 1. The same is true for the city where he lives, so the country and the city where he lives. I take it that it's perfectly clear to all parties where the sensitive issue lies. That was at least one issue, Mr. Saxon. Was there another administrative issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour, and the Prosecution believes it may be best to move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the assistance of the usher to escort Witness 1 into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, while we're waiting for the witness to appear, the Prosecution has prepared a set of binders for the parties and for Your Honours with the exhibits that the Prosecution will seek to tender in this case. Perhaps they could be distributed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, of course, we usually have the assistance of the usher who just left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness 1. I call you "Witness 1" because the Chamber has decided that we'll not call you in open court by your own name, not primarily because you were seeking protection but for other reasons. May I, first of all, ask you not to use your own name until and unless it's clear that we are in private or closed session. Witness 1, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you by the usher; but before you make that solemn declaration, I'd like to ask you whether you speak English at such a level that you can follow the proceedings and that you're able to answer questions in the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then may I invite you to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Witness 1. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 1, you'll now be examined by Mr. Saxon, who's counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness 1.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I also understand that sometimes your hearing is not absolutely perfect, so if you do not completely hear a question that you are asked, please tell me, or if the volume needs to be turned up for your headphones, please inform me, and we will take care of that. All right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One reminder, please, I'd like to ask you during your testimony not to refer to the country where you live and work, and not to refer and not to refer to the city where you live and work. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, I will try my best on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The other thing I would like to ask you, you and I are now speaking the same language. We're speaking to each other in English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we need to be careful to assist the interpreters that each person that we don't begin to speak until the other person has stopped speaking; and if you could, perhaps try to pause for a moment between sentences to give the interpreters a minute to -- a moment to catch up. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, officially, you are still a member of the police in your country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, would it not be wise, at least in whatever way not known to the public, to establish the identity of the witness, either by a pseudonym sheet or by going into private session; otherwise, we would not know who Witness 1 is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Completely my oversight, Your Honour. Yes. We have a pseudonym sheet prepared; and if this could be provided to the usher to give to the witness, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 1, is that your true name on that sheet of paper in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is the date of birth correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, perhaps the pseudonym sheet could become part of the record in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually, exhibit numbers are assigned to it. Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the Defence wish to have a look at the pseudonym sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm fully willing to accept that it's the correct name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Same for you, Mr. Dieckmann?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I join, yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, this would be exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number P1, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that there are also no objections against P1; therefore, P1 is admitted into evidence under seal. Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 1, when did you begin your career as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in July of 2007, last year, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: I was detective superintendent and a head of the witness protection unit for the western part of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was the protected witness in this case one of the persons under the responsibility of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 1, in early July of 2007, was the protected witness scheduled to travel somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you drive the witness to the airport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the drive to the airport, what, if anything, did the protected witness inform you about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. He informed me that he received telephone contact and communication by SMS as well as regular phone call from a person he'd known as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the protected witness tell you the name of the journalist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was that name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: It's sort of Morina or something like that. I'm not sure about the pronouncement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And did the protected witness inform you of the nature of these telephone communications?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, can you describe what the protected witness told you at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: He told me that this journalist would like to have a meeting with the protected witness; and the day after this meeting, he suggest that also -- or he told me that minister of culture as well would attend to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Did the protected witness inform you why Mr. Morina and the minister of culture wanted to meet with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, because I asked the protected witness why, what was this conversation all about, since my responsibility was his safety and his appearance here in the court. So I was curious and a little bit suspicious about this call, and I asked the protected witness to get back to the journalist and ask him what this meeting was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we go further, there's a question I forgot to ask you. Were there any particular questions, according to the protected witness, that Mr. Morina asked that caused you some concern?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. He let the protected witness -- the journalist let the protected witness know that he knows that he's supposed to go down to the Tribunal in The Hague to take the stand as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Tribunal in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: And that makes me worry because no one should know that we are on our way down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. If we can turn now to a question I asked you previously, did the protected witness explain why Mr. Morina and the minister wanted to meet with the protected witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No, because the journalist won't talk about the real purpose over the phone, and that made me more suspicious about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 1, did the protected witness tell you whether he wanted to meet with Mr. Morina and the minister?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. He was curious about what they want him, and he really likes this meeting to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did he tell you why he was curious?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No -- yes. He said, "I don't know what they really want and I'm anxious to hear about it."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Witness 1, what concerns, if any, did you have about such a meeting taking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: I don't like it because my responsibility was to see that the protected witness really fulfilled his duty and come here to the Tribunal and take the witness-stand. That's the first responsibility. The other one was for his and his family's security before and after this stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so -- all right. Did you discuss the situation with your superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With whom did you discuss this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: The chief constable, who is my chief, and I tell him I don't like this meeting because if there is legitimate reasons, they could tell it on the phone. But since they don't mention what it is all about, I get suspicious that they try to provide or even buy [Realtime transcript read in error "by"] this witness silence; otherwise, they could have tell him what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, you took a risk by asking the witness with whom did you discuss, instead of what was the position of the person you discussed it with. Well, nothing happened, but I'm just trying to keep you as sharp as possible on the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I'm very grateful for that, Your Honour. The point is well taken. Just to note for the record, at page 32, line 13, the word by is spelled b-y and it should be spelled b-u-y.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how did the chief constable react to the idea of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: He didn't like it at all. He said the police force will not - what do you call? - be at -- let this witness have a meeting who could stop him from going to the Tribunal in Hague. So he said at the first no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And after you spoke first with the chief constable and received his opinion, did you tell the protected witness how the chief constable felt about this matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. I told him the decision and I told him also that the police cannot allow this meeting to happen because it can interfere with his mission down here. And he was not -- he's not taking this message well because he said, "I certainly like to have this meeting. And if I don't -- can have this meeting, I will not appear in The Hague Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say, "I will not appear in The Hague Tribunal," the witness was saying, I will not testify; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Oh, that's correct, that's correct. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you received this reaction from the protected witness, did you convey that to the chief constable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, I get back to him and said, "We have a big problem here because I can't fulfil my responsibility." And chief constable said, "The only way the police can allow this meeting is that we had to be there, and certainly the Prosecutions -- Prosecutors in Hague had to write a letter saying that we will assist them; otherwise, we don't do it."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go a little bit more slowly. When you say the chief constable said, "The only way the police can allow this meeting is that we had to be there," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: We had to monitoring this meeting; we have to get totally control of the area, the surveillance team; we have to film it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you have to record it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then you mentioned something about what the chief constable wanted from the Prosecutors in The Hague. Can you describe that again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, because that was the only way that he could let this meeting happen. The Prosecutor had to write a letter to the chief constable saying that they like this meeting to happen and they will have the police assistance for this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So, in other words, the chief constable wanted a letter from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Saying that the meeting could take place if it's monitored --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- by the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask all this evidence is in dispute in various regards that my learned friend not lead at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't really trying to lead. I was trying to make sure that the English transcript comes up -- is as clear as possible because English is not the witness's first language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that. Of course, if clarification is needed, perhaps the question can simply be re-put without trying to summarize what the witness has already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, you're invited not to lead in chief. As guidance, I would like you to follow the suggestion by Mr. Khan. At the same time, I invite Mr. Khan not to be oversensitive. By leading it is often very practical; but, of, course there are some sensitive issues on which you're invited to be very strict on not leading. I leave it to you, Mr. Khan, to make objections only if really need, and you to be very cautious in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Eventually, did the OTP -- did the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal provide such a written letter to the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to the initial meeting, what arrangements or precautions, if any, did you and your police colleagues take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: We have first at the airport personnel that meet the plane who the journalist arrived with. We checked the other passengers on the plane before and that plane and the plane later, to see if there was any connection that we know of. We followed the journalist from the airport to the town. We have the surveillance team, we have the film team, we have a recording team; and I think at least we were about 30 officers at the place totally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you coordinating this effort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of the coordinators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the protected witness agree that the meeting would be recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall, please, when did the first meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: I think it was around the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And who was expected to appear for that first meeting, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: It was the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know if the minister was ever expected to appear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, because we had a request from protected witness that we should book a room for the minister the day two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, at page 36 -- actually, I should go more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said "that we should book a room for the minister the day two." What do you mean by "the day two"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Oh, for the 11th of July --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: -- the day after the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 1, in general terms, where did the first meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: In a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe how the first meeting was monitored?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. We had some officers around the lobby area in that hotel, we have a film team outside, and we also have put two microphones to the protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What do you mean by putting two microphones to the protected witness? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: There was two microphones. I don't know if I had to go into the details where we placed microphones because it's kind of an operational secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may assist my learned friend. There's no dispute from the Defence about the surveillance or the recording. There's no dispute. He can just move to the central issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much then. I will move along then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's appreciated, Mr. Khan, that you assisted Mr. Saxon. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 1, when, if ever, did you see the journalist Morina around the time of the first meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: I actually saw him visually as he come through the doors to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned "day two." What happened on day two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: We changed hotels for the second meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: -- late that morning, but it's nearby, about 500 metres from the first hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was that the day after the first meeting on the 10th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And what was your role before and during the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: My role was the same as on the first meeting, so it was planning and get the surveillance team and monitoring on the right place for the second meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Prior to these meetings in July 2007, had you been involved in surveillance and recording conversations before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was it important that -- let me step back for a minute. And why had you been involved in surveillance and recording conversations many times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Because I was the head of the surveillance unit that concerns kidnapping, blackmailing, and such things in serious crime business.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Was it important that the protected witness agree to the recording of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Because when somebody agreed or want his own conversation recorded, that's totally legal in my country, so that's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the hour. I was about to turn to an exhibit that might take a few minutes. Would this be the right time to take the first break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be preferable to have the break now. But before we take the break could I just, Mr. Khan, verify with you, you said there's no dispute from the Defence about the surveillance or the reporting. What does that include?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it wasn't very artfully put. There's no dispute that the exhibit that the Prosecution wish to tender and the transcript is -- well, there's no dispute that a video was obtained and a transcript was prepared. So there was no need to go into details about where the microphones were situated or how many people were located in which particular parts of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: (redacted) That's a separate issue which has been ruled upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then take it that the exhibit you just referred to, that you accept that these exhibits are the result of the audio-recording, and that of other exhibits are pictures of the meetings that were recorded, and do you take any issue with the content of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. There's simply one issue that's already been litigated in relation to part of it, and it's really the transcript. It's a separate matter, it doesn't concern this witness, it's made later -- it will be made later. But apart from that, no dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No dispute. Mr. Saxon, is this clear enough for you to know what is not in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then have a break now, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very, very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Smith has just pointed out there may be a need for a redaction, page 39, line 8, and that that should happen I believe before we take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that should be redacted. Mr. Registrar, could you prepare a redaction of page 39, lines 7, 8, and 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, line 8 only the first two-thirds. We can leave the last sentence of the observation made by Mr. Khan. I prefer to finalise it before we have the break and then we'll resume at 11.00. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness Number 1, I would like to show you a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether the second exhibit binder could be placed in front of the witness. And, Your Honour, I'm going to ask the witness to look at what is Prosecution 65 ter Exhibit Number 29. It should be at tab 29 and will be in your second binder, and I'd ask that this not be published to the public, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, again, for the -- hopefully to assist, we can agree, as far as the Defence is concerned, that that picture shows the two people mentioned in the Prosecution's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Mr. Khan, and would Mr. Khan also be willing to make the same agreement for 65 ter number 30 which is another photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, if that's the case, I don't need to ask the witness about this -- actually, I do, Your Honour. I'm very, very sorry. I do have one question I need to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness, if you take a look at what is 65 ter 29, this photograph, do you recognise someone in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The man to the right on the photo is the protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recognise the place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. It is in the lobby where the first meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now seek to tender this exhibit, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And now you asked these questions only about 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will ask the same questions for 30 as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, first of all ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move any further, Judge Moloto has one further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness 1, are you able to say who the person to the left is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not on this photo, no, I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Just for the record, I would like to say that the Defence for Bajrush Morina join the submissions of the Defence of Astrit Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Then, Mr. Registrar, 65 ter number 29 was, although declared not admissible, is not yet in evidence. So, therefore, Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 29 would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P2, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2 under seal. And from the previous comments, I take it there are no objections -- any further objections, because the whole of the recording, of course, was part of an objection once. P2 is admitted into evidence under seal. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 1, if you could turn to the next exhibit, please, the next tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter number 30.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you able to recognise the place in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, I am. It's the hotel lobby for the second meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise any of the persons in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No, not really, because there's no good quality on the clearness, so I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You say there's no good quality on the clearness. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: It is so much grey in this photo, it's difficult to hundred per cent said something about --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would seek to tender into evidence 65 ter number 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal, as well, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Under seal, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The same is true for this, exhibit on the 65 ter list, earlier declared to be not inadmissible. Mr. Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P3, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3 is admitted under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 1, prior to the first meeting between the protected witness and the journalist Morina, what, if anything, did the protected witness say about SMS telephone messages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: For the most telephone or SMS the protected witness received, he immediately tells or show us on the phone, and there was quite a lot of traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the witness tell you or show you who sent those messages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: It's from the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you become aware of the content of one or more of those messages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. There was especially one I remember because the protected witness said that he had to book a room for the 11th for the minister of culture, and he would like a hotel with a high standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: And there was also some sort of -- that the minister really would come because I have some suspicion about these arrivals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you clarify what you just said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. It was kind of confirmed -- he confirmed that the minister really should come day two, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: -- he asked especially for some quality of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. In such cases, Witness 1, what procedure, if any, would police in your country carry out to preserve such SMS messages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Well, we emptied normally the phone to save both the SMS and the telephone traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you be a little bit more specific. What do you mean when you say we "emptied" the phone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: We have a kind of operation box that we put on the phone, and we take it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What then comes out of this box?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: What comes is time, when it was sent, and when it was received, or what kind of number if possible, who sent them, and the text on the SMS as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with binder number 1, I would be very grateful. And if we could turn, please, to what is Prosecution 65 ter number 12.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the witness's microphone be adjusted so that he speaks into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, before we turn to tab 12, Mr. Usher, can you just wait a minute. Please, just wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned the procedure that the police would carry out to preserve SMS messages. Was this procedure followed in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, as I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was a copy of the SMS messages given to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: As I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn now to Exhibit Number 12, it should be tab 12 in that binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, very practically, exhibits on this list 7 up to and including 23 have been admitted as attachments to a 92 ter statement already. They have, however, not been provided yet with assigned numbers, exhibit numbers. Mr. Registrar, how to proceed? Could you assign ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest the following. Since we're now dealing with 65 ter number 12, that Mr. Registrar assigns a number to it; and to the extent that you will deal with certain exhibits that are already admitted, that immediately Mr. Registrar assigns a number to them. And those exhibits not further dealt with in court, that Mr. Registrar makes an internal memorandum assigning numbers to them, so that, finally, we know where they are on our exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 12 becomes Exhibit Number P4, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P4 under seal. It was admitted already so it's just an administrative exercise now to assign a number to it. P4 under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 1, could you take a moment, please, read through the English text, these messages, and tell us if any of these messages -- if the contents of any of these messages are familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Many of those was more of a grey thing -- sort, as they have a family aspect, but there is 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop there for a moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Number 39 comes from the telephone 37744506183?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "Hello my friend! Can you make a hotel reservation for me for the 10th and 11th and for the minister only for the 11th of July?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the date is the 7th. It appears to be -- appears to be the 6th of July, then, of 2007?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What do you recall about this message? Why do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: I recall it because it confirms that the minister really should come, and also I see under 36 there is this same kind of thing I also have been told about and I recall it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after 39, any other messages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, 42, it was kind of confirmed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the record, number 42 says, from the same telephone number as before: "One a while ago together. See you there on 10 July." And it appears to be from the 2nd of July. Can you turn the page. Are there any other messages that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, 43, and that is what I told you before, that the quality of hotel for the minister was an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for the record, message 43, from the same telephone number, from the 7th of July, 2007, says: "We'll talk on the phone on Monday, or you make a reservation today. Bear in mind, though, that this Haraqija is 'choosey' and wouldn't just accept to stay at any hotel. E-mail the hotel address to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And now that binder can be removed -- actually -- yes, that binder can be removed, please. Then if the second binder could be given back to the witness, and if the witness could turn, please, to tab 24H. Your Honours, this will be Prosecution 65 ter 24H. And, actually, Mr. Usher, I'm going to need your assistance for a moment or two with the witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- number 2005/06: 178, and entitled --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have misspoken. At page 48, line 20, there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is entitled: "Secret wire-tapping of rooms," and it says that: "The Government is handing over this proposition to the Parliament ... on the 16th of March, 2006 ..." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it's from the justice department of your country. And now if the usher could help you, and if you could turn, please, to what is page 48 in your language. The page numbers are pretty small, they're up on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this should not be published to the public. It has ERN number 06360579.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could, please, Witness 1, skim down the page a little bit, and you'll see in the middle of the page, in your version, you'll see a sentence beginning with the words: "Here, the notion ..." or "Here, the idea ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I believe I can show you where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, will you take that to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to read that sentence and a couple more sentences to you in English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says: "Here, the notion 'in secret' means that all people participating in the conversation are unaware of the room being wire-tapped. Should one of the participants be aware of the room being wire-tapped, then it is not a question of secret wire-tapping of rooms, but some other measure for which there is admittedly no explicit support in law but that is not punishable (either) according to chapter 4, section 9a in the Criminal Code." Have you been following me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Earlier today, page 38, lines 16 to 17, you told the Chamber that it's legal in your country to record conversations between two parties if one party agrees to the recording. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question for you is: Is the concept expressed here in this proposition consistent with how the police in your country carry out surveillance or inconsistent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You didn't listen to my question. You need to just listen to my entire question. I asked you: Is it consistent or inconsistent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: It's consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would seek to tender 65 ter number 24H and I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No. Mr. Saxon, do you think that there would have been a possibility to resolve 24I where you read one or two pages but instead produce approximately half a wood in paper format? I'm just asking you because I see that we get a hundred pages where you rely on one. Would there, then, have not been any possibility to agree with the Defence that the page you just read is sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With a cover page, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. And in the language of the witness, it would be, yeah, page 48, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. But my question is: Would there not have been another solution than to just present us with hundred pages where 98 pages are totally superfluous?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
