utterances.text: I take your point, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you're invited to reorganize this exhibit in such a way that the relevant pages are where we can then admit them; that is, cover page and the relevant page you just read from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, we combine the two exhibits, 24H and I, with, as a matter of fact, 24H being the translation of the relevant portion of 24I. So we'll ask Mr. Registrar to assign a number to the two of them, and then you're invited to just limit the non-English version in such a way that it doesn't take a hundred pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 24H and the relevant portion of 24I will become Exhibit Number P5, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P5 is admitted under seal. Please proceed. And, Mr. Saxon, we'll hear from you what pages you exactly now are tendering in the original language.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Witness 1, you'll now be cross-examined by Defence counsel, but I do not know whether they have agreed on the sequence. Mr. Dieckmann, will you be the first one to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We agreed that I will take the lead with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Witness 1, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Dieckmann, who's counsel for Mr. Morina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: A very good morning --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: -- Witness 1. My name is Jens Dieckmann. I'm Defence counsel for Mr. Bajrush Morina, and I have a couple of questions for you. First of all, I also would like to stress if you have any problems to understand my questions, please indicate it immediately and I could rephrase or repeat them. Witness number 1, you've been responsible as a police officer for the Witness Number 2, it's true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Since when have you been responsible, could you just illustrate it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, I don't recall, but it's several months before his travel down to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. You did it together with other colleagues, or have you been the only one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You have been the first contact for the protected witness in cases of problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to go in private session because I would like to refer to colleagues and as would be proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: In the meanwhile, we received a so-called proofing notice from the Prosecution from the 6th of September, and I may summarize it where it's stated that: "The protected witness suggested to you that perhaps they wanted to prevent him from testifying," end of my summary of quotation. Do you remember this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very sorry to interrupt, but just so I could follow along with my colleague, could he tell me which page, which paragraph he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've now found it. It is the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering whether a copy could be provided to the witness, Your Honour. I have brought multiple copies in case the witness would like to follow along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, any objection against the witness being provided with a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No objections. It is just one sentence I would like to ask him, but, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Today you testified, and I refer to page 31, line 7 of the provisional transcript, and I may quote: "The journalist let the protected witness know that he's supposed to go down to the Tribunal in The Hague to be a protected witness," end of quotation from page 31, line 7. So from your testimony today, it seems that Bajrush Morina should have a qualified knowledge about that what should happen in The Hague. I would like to ask you what is the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Because when we would travel down with a protected witness, it was for a meeting with the Prosecutors down here. It wasn't actually for -- to appear here in the Tribunal court. And that's why I was a little bit suspicious that it has been a leak that he will be going down The Hague. So I was a little bit suspicious about the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Did the protected witness explicitly said that Bajrush Morina has known that he is a witness in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No. As I recall he said, "As I know, you are travelling down to the Tribunal in Hague." That's what I recall from this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. As a result of this conversation with the protected witness in the beginning of July 2007, you spoke to your superiors you told us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And, first of all, your superiors refused to give in the wish of the protected witness to have this meeting; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And the immediate and first reaction of the protected witness was that he told you that he would not testify if the meeting did not take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And, finally, your superiors accepted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: After he had received a letter from the Prosecutors down in Hague; otherwise, it had -- the meeting wouldn't go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So, if the Prosecutor had disagreed, the superiors of you would not have accepted the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No. There would be no meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So we can summarize in the end, there was a condense [sic] of the Prosecution of the ICTY, your superiors, and the witness that this meeting could take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: The protected witness was curious you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And he was not afraid from your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No. Why I remember that is when I told him the police chief constable would not allow this meeting for safety and such, the protected witness said, "Hey, if there is something dangerous around this, they wouldn't have called me first," so that's why I can refer to that he was not afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And being responsible for the surveying measures that had taken place on the 10th of July and the 11th of July, have you had a chance to listen to the recordings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No, because that was on a language that I don't know nothing about. So I just heard the quality and that's good enough for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you have seen the video?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Just some results of it, not the whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: But have you been in the moment on the 10th and 11th of July participating in the surveying measures and visiting what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Just for some seconds, and then I get back because we didn't let anyone know that we were around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: From your long-term experience as a police officer being occupied with protective measures like this, do you agree with me that audio recordings of private conversations basically constitute a violation of the right of privacy of a person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. Due to your experience and knowledge, it was not necessary to have an order of a court to allow you this under the law of your country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Not that specific meeting because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- we had no criminal case against any one of those. If that had been the matter, then we have take -- have decisions from the prosecutor and the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very sorry to interrupt. The country of the witness is referred to in page 66, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you just refer to the page and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- ask for a redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Page 66, line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 66, line 8 to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry for this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: In the proofing note from 6 September 2008 and also today, you refer, explaining us the legal basis for the police actions to Prosecution Exhibit 24, I think, I, where the leading principles of the law of your home country for this kind of bugging should be expressed. Witness Number 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think, at this point, it would be helpful to the witness to have his proofing note in front of him. We're getting into a technical area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A copy of the proofing note may be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if my colleague could indicate to the witness what paragraph he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I refer to page 2 and the fourth paragraph from above.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, since it becomes a legal debate rather than a witness examination, the Chamber might be interested in having a copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, would the Chamber like to mark this for identification in some way so there's a record of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see how it will be used and then consider marking it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I refer especially to the sentence, I may quote: "It is not against the law in GN's country to record conversations in this manner as long as one of the persons involved in the conversation knows it is being recorded. Witness 1 confirmed that this principle is expressed in Prosecution Exhibit 24I." Witness number 1, are you aware that this reference you've made is just a government proposition and not a law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. But it's the kind of opposite, because it says there is no support from law to convict somebody to record his own conversation. So it's not against the law, simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: But, finally, you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at one of the previous questions and the answers given to that. Witness 1, a question was put to you earlier, and I'll read it literally to you. "From your long-term experience as a police officer being occupied with protective measures like this, do you agree with me that audio-recordings of private conversations basically constitute a violation of the rights of privacy of a person?" And your answer was: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to read what your question is. Yes. I thought the question was about the privacy, that is a law against integrity and such things, that's why I answered yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you now tell us that you consider it not to be illegal, and at the same time you tell us that it basically constitutes a violation of the right of privacy of a person. My first question would be: Focusing on the present situation, whose privacy would be violated or whose right of privacy would be violated in the present context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's easy for me if I can express. There is two things concerning this matter with monitoring with -- and recording this kind of conversation. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... then you have to have decision from prosecutor and court. But in this case, there was no cause because this matter was up to the department of justice in my home country, concerning if somebody broke a law intend to attempt the witness. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now we have a situation that we had no suspicious, no criminal case against anyone for that department have tell us. So now it was concerning the protected witness's safety and his wishes to record this conversation, and that is legally no problem in my home country. I can't go into -- I couldn't express myself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, this is what happens if you ask legal opinions from a witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just have two final questions regarding this matter, if I'm allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Witness Number 1, do you agree with me that in July 2007, there was no provision in the legislation, in the law of your country allowing audio-recordings of private conversations, secret wire-tapping of rooms, and bugging of persons, no written law passed by the parliament?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: There was no law against it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. And last question to this aspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question. Mr. Dieckmann is interested to know whether there was any law which would give a legal basis for such operations. You said there was no law prohibiting it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that this included that apart from there being no law prohibiting it, that there was also no law providing a legal basis for such wire-tapping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, I just referred to the law text that I had before me here, there is no law support to convict anyone recording his own conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, whether it's a criminal offence is again another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Dieckmann, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: So you could confirm that these audio-tapes and the videos have been produced under the rules of surveying the security of person not as a part of the criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And it's correct that you handed over this material you have recorded to the ICTY Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Did you do it voluntarily or did the Prosecutor from the ICTY ask you to give them the material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: I asked them if they want this recording sent down here, because we -- all the material was played into CD, four of it. And I ask the Prosecutors down here if they like it to send over it, and they say, "Thank you. Immediately, please." And I travel myself to the airport and hand it over to a captain on a KLM flight, and the Prosecutors or investigators down here meet the aeroplane in Amsterdam, Schiphol.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Did you hand over the material with special conditions of confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this question to these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, if you want to explain anything which might influence the witness in his answer, then we would have to ask the witness to leave the courtroom; but if you can explain without any such fact, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: We are referring to the point that this material was used later on in the proceeding against our clients, and we are interested in the conditions under what this material was handed over to the Prosecution and which knowledge the Prosecution has had about the nature and the origin of this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question. Would you please tell us whether any conditions were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- put by the Office of the Prosecution, and conditions put by you to the Office of the Prosecution, when you handed over these materials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was, as I said, four CDs packed in each plastic and was taped and in a package, and I showed them to the captain on the KLM, so he was sure it was nothing else. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 1, it is about conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Conditions such as use it only on Wednesdays or whatever conditions you added to the hand-over of this material.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I call -- can I say the name of the investigator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Investigator of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think that there is any problem, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a man called Barney, and I called him and I said, They are on the way," and he will meet the aeroplane at the Schiphol. So it goes from me to the captain to the Barney, and then I don't know anything else about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No further conditions like use it only for this purpose or use it only for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: May I conclude that you did not inform the ICTY Prosecutors about the nature of or the -- the nature of this material, that this material was produced only in the procedure of protecting the security and not being part of a criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. There was just -- because I didn't listen to the material. I said, This is for you, we don't need it, we have no criminal case in my country. So it's yours, do what you like."

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You told the ICTY Prosecutors that this -- that there is no criminal procedure in your country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get informations from the ICTY Prosecution that the contempt procedure was initiated at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: I have to read. Yes. I read the letter down to my chief of constable that I require that this meeting would take place, so I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann. Could I seek clarification of the last answer. The question was whether you got information from the ICTY Prosecution that the contempt procedure was initiated at the ICTY. You said: "Yes. I read the letter down to my chief ..." What letter are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring -- maybe I don't understand the contempt procedure on the question before. I understand your question if I know that the Prosecutors down here would let this meeting happen, and that's my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's clear there is a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether - and the question was put to you without any time-frame - whether you were aware that proceedings, which I understand to be investigation and then prosecution, for contempt of court - that is, in this case, the suspicion that there was interference with witnesses - had been initiated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so, because when I talked to the Prosecutor witnesses [sic], I said I don't understand the language, and he give me the information that there was something in this recording that would have sort of stopped his witness and -- but I don't get into details. That's something for the Prosecutors down here, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that after you'd given the material or before you had given the material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it after the meetings had taken place or before the meetings on the 10th and the 11th of July had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So between the meetings when everything was recorded and before giving it to the Prosecutor's office at the ICTY, you informed them about the content. Is that how I have to understand your answer; that is, that there was in the discussion about, as you said, something in this recording that would sort of stopped this witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sort of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they then inform you about whether they would proceed against these persons, whether they intended to investigate, or whether they intended to prosecute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My -- as I recall it, they were interested in and listen to this record and then come back. So there was no clearance that they should have a case as I recall, but they certainly like to listen to the recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers and clarification of the last question and answer that was put to you by Mr. Dieckmann. Mr. Khan, any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You'll be glad to know I have only a few questions, so hopefully you can go home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Khan, and I apologise for interrupting, the LiveNote technical issue has been resolved. The settings are now as they should be. But most likely you would have to restart LiveNote to get these new settings on your screens; otherwise, it will still be the old situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, you've told the Court that your overriding aim in all of this was to ensure that the witness would come to the court here in The Hague and also ensure that his family was protected. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And in discharging these functions, you also knew that he was protected by order of this Court; you knew that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I suppose, being a very experienced police officer and the head of your witness scheme, you would have seen the terms of the protective order issued by the Trial Chamber of this Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You had misgivings about the meeting that the witness was so keen to have; that's fair, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And you discussed your anxiety with superiors within your ministry and your immediate superior; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And this meeting was conditioned. According to your superior, the condition for it to go ahead was the permission of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The order of protection was not issued by the Prosecutor; you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Sorry, the last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The order giving protective measures to this particular witness was not something simply requested by the Prosecutor; it was an order of a Trial Chamber. You are aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And your responsibility, I presume, was to ensure the Trial Chamber's order was fully honoured and respected? I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, why didn't you go to the Trial Chamber and ask the Trial Chamber for permission to commence this surveillance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: The reason why is that when we come here the first week in July, the only one I met was Prosecutor and investigators or witness protection people down here. So I didn't know no one else to contact when this matter comes up. So it's personal contact, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's very candid. Thank you. When you spoke to the Prosecution and told them about the conversation between Mr. Morina and the protected witness, the Prosecution were similarly concerned; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did, in fact, they tell you that they were concerned that there had been a lot of witness intimidation in this case and they thought that a similar attempt may be tried now in relation to this protected witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: You know, before this meeting was going on, we didn't exactly know. It was just suspicions we have, and it was unnaturally communication that get us on this trial. So we didn't know actually, but we suspected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And that's what I'm going towards. You suspected -- let me rephrase it. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm listening and Mr. Registrar is always listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: When you had conversations with the Office of the Prosecution here in The Hague and mentioned the phone call between Mr. Morina and the protected witness, is it fair to say that the Prosecution thought that an attempt may be in the offing --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe this question is calling for a lot of speculation, Your Honour, the way it's phrased right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can rephrase it. In my respectful submission, before you rule, I'm -- my question is predicated upon the conversation the witness says in evidence he had with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, if you say you can rephrase it, let's do it, so then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Forgive me, Witness, for the bad question. The Prosecution told you, did they not, that they were concerned that there may be an attempt to intimidate this protected witness that was in your care? That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No. They were curious about this meeting as well. No one actually said something straightly out because we didn't know; but there was interest in this meeting, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thirty people were involved to satisfy your curiosity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No. It was because we didn't know. It had to be -- since the police said yes to the Prosecutor's request about this meeting, we had to take measures. Nothing whatsoever happened during this meeting. That's why we -- it was a lot of people surrounding this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You said earlier, and perhaps I misunderstood you, that in your country --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: -- if this -- and correct me if I'm wrong. I think it was page 69 or thereabouts under the original LiveNote transcript. But you said that if this had been a criminal case (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: If this -- if you had suspicions and this had been a witness in your home country, would you have sought an order from a Trial Chamber in order to commence this video and audio surveillance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes. That's why we take contact with the justice of department, just to see that we don't have a criminal case in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm very grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. Khan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, any need to further examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness 1, my colleague just asked you the following question: "If you had suspicions and this had been a witness in your home country, would you have sought an order from a Trial Chamber in order to commence this video and audio surveillance?" You answered: "Yes. That's why we take contact with the justice department, just to see that we don't have a criminal case in this." Can you explain that a little bit more, please. Did you or your office contact the justice department of your country for advice in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, by the chief constable get to the national board and then to the justice of department, just to see that The Hague Tribunal is not a court in the law of my home country's meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And that was confirmed by the justice department of your country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. My learned colleague asked you a few minutes ago, he asked you whether 30 people were involved in surveillance of these meetings in order to satisfy your curiosity. Can you refresh our memories again, what were your two responsibilities in this matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: One was to see that the protected witness fulfil his duty and give testimony at the Tribunal in Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You need to move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: All right. That was the first responsibility. The second one is his and his family's safety before, under, and after this statement in Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is that why you felt you needed a large team of people to carry out the surveillance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, because we didn't know what this was. It was an attempt to get the protected witness forward, in the open, and maybe hurt him in any way, because we had to take all precautions. We are this hundred per cent. That's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What do you mean, "We are this hundred per cent"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: You have to be a hundred per cent sure that nothing is happening to the witness; and since we agreed to the meeting and take him to the meeting, we had to make sure nothing happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the witness understood this as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just one more question, and this is really just an adjustment of the transcript. A few minutes ago the Presiding Judge, Judge Orie, on page 75, line 6 -- excuse me, lines 3 to 4, asked you whether you were aware whether this Tribunal was bringing contempt proceedings in this matter. And you said, you answered at line 6: "Yes, I suppose so. When I spoke to Prosecution witnesses ..." and then you said, "I didn't understand the language, so he gave me information." Were you referring to Prosecution witnesses or someone else? Did you speak with Prosecution witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: No, no, no. I had to misunderstand something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who were you referring to when you said "I spoke to Prosecution ..."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ah, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question or a short series of questions to you, Witness 1. You earlier said that if there would be a criminal case, you would have sought an order or permission by the court under your domestic law to engage in an exercise as you did. Now, if I understood you well, we are here in a situation in which it is considered a possibility on the basis of little information, the information being that the protected witness, was aware that someone knew that he would travel to The Hague. Would that create already a criminal case for which you would seek a court order, or would that be so much in the initial stages where the suspicion had only a limited basis that you would first further explore the suspicion? Could you tell us what approximately in your system would apply?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: If this has been against a court in my home country, then, as we did now, we check with the prosecutors and my chief, do we have a case; and if that was it, we have taking permission from prosecutors and the court to have this recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would you consider here to be sufficient information available to have a case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you mean by "a case," a suspicion sufficiently solid to proceed the investigations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you call "have a case"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So reason to proceed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And to find further evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One final question. In order to have a case, is there a need that the offence has already been committed, or would having a case also include a situation in which there is a risk or a chance, a relevant chance, that the offence will be committed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: I have to look. There's a risk. If there is a risk, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is sufficient to have a case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 1
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions of the Bench triggered any need to put further questions to the witness? If not, Witness 1, this concludes your testimony today. I'd like to thank you very much for having come and having answered the questions of the parties and of the Bench. You are excused. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry for my English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there's no reason I would say to apologise. [The witness withdrew].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is time for a break. We'll have a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, a few procedural matters. The first one, as the parties are aware of, the request for certification is denied by the Chamber; that means that the Chamber has decided to deny that. The reasons will be given in an oral presentation of this decision, including reasons then, most likely tomorrow. Further, the Chamber, I think, needs all of its breaks to keep a close eye on request for reconsideration. I haven't read them yet. I do see that one or two such requests are pending. We'll read them and then we'll see how to proceed with those requests. Finally, the proofing notes of Witness 1, there was a request to have it marked for identification. The Chamber doesn't really see at this moment a need to do that because everything that was put to the witness was read out to him. So, unless the parties would make further submissions why it is necessary to have this marked for identification, the Chamber will not proceed as suggested and leave it as it is. Mr. Saxon, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution will now call Witness Number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and he will testify in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not in closed session --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but I think it was pseudonym and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Facial distortion and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- face and voice distortion. The voice distortion needs some time to prepare. Have these preparations been made?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. I see the equipment there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, for face and voice distortion, the curtains have to be down as the witness enters the courtroom and then they can be raised again. Mr. Saxon, I think that the 92 ter statements appearing as 65 ter numbers 3 and 4 are admitted into evidence already, although no number has yet been assigned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, if you tender them, would you please draw my attention to that so that the number will be assigned to the 92 ter statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps, while we're waiting, whether binder number 1 might be placed on the desk where the witness will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, again --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The usher is not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usher is not present. That's what they call multi-tasking these days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 2, because that's how we will call you in these proceedings, Witness 2, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Usher, could you please hand out the text of the solemn declaration. And may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Witness 2, the protective measures that were earlier granted to you - that is, testimony to be given under pseudonym and face and voice distortion - still do apply. Please take care that in answering questions, that you do not refer to your identity and also not to the state in which you reside or the city in which you live or any other reference to that state in any way. You'll first be examined by Mr. Saxon, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Saxon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we have prepared a piece of paper with the witness's details on them, if that could be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness Number 2. Witness Number 2, can you please take a look at that piece of paper in front of you and let us know whether your name is written there correctly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is your date of birth written there correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes, it is. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this sheet could be shown to my colleagues from the Defence; and if there is no objection, then I would seek to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has looked at it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No objection as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the pseudonym sheet would be exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P6, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6 is admitted under seal. May I remind everyone that microphones should be switched off when the witness answers the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering if I could ask for the kind assistance of our usher again, if binder number 1 could be placed in front of the witness, please, and if it could be opened to tab number 3, which, Your Honour, was Prosecution 65 ter 3 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness Number 2, you'll see that there is a statement placed in front of you; it has your name on it. Are you looking at it in the Albanian version, because that is the version that you've signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall providing this statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 14th of August of last year, 2007?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are the contents of this written statement true and correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does this written statement reflect what you would say if you were examined or questioned verbally here in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, at this time, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we also ask the witness whether -- you said it's true and accurate. Does it reflect the statement you gave on the 14th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I think we only have to, apart from -- I made a mistake, as a matter of fact, and I asked whether you had any objections; whereas, it's admitted already into evidence. So I apologise for that. But it has not yet received a number. 65 ter number 3, Mr. Registrar, would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P7, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7 was already admitted into evidence. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Witness, if you could please turn to the next tab in that binder, which is tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be 65 ter number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could turn to the Albanian version, please, Witness Number 2, this is another statement bearing your name and signature. It's dated the 20th of September, 2007. Do you recall giving this statement to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall that yesterday you reviewed the Albanian version of this statement in my office, in the company of myself and an interpreter and an OTP investigator? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you turn to paragraph 23, please. Witness Number 2, is there anything in paragraph 23 that you feel should be corrected?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes. I think something should be added or corrected here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what that correction should be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: I will try to explain. In the second part of the paragraph reference is made to -- that Haraqija should not contact me because there were three people who would be very important, who could give critical evidence against Haradinaj, one of whom was the protected witness, the second one was Bujar Bukoshi, and the third one Halil Bicaj, former minister of defence. I asked Bajrush whether Bicaj was the third person and he said, "No, I don't think so." At one point, Bajrush told me that Schook told Haraqija that these three can save Haradinaj by not testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to interrupt you there. So the correction in this paragraph, in the last two or three sentences, it should simply say that, during your meeting, Mr. Morina referred to yourself, Mr. Bukoshi, and an unnamed third person, rather than Mr. Halil Bicaj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then, at some point, you asked Mr. Morina if Mr. Bicaj was the third person and Mr. Morina said: "No, I did not think so." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then, so with those changes, would this paragraph be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just as a point of clarification, you mentioned earlier something about that: "... Haraqija should not contact me because there were three people ..." Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: No, that's not exactly what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: I wanted to say that in the last sentence, where it is said that these three people could save Haradinaj by not testifying, that the name of the third person should not be mentioned as Halil Bicaj because he had said that that was not the third person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Bajrushi had said that that was not the third person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Bajrush say that was not the third person or that he did not think so or did not know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: I asked him could Halil Bicaj be the third person, and he said: "No, I don't think so."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness Number 2, with that correction in paragraph 23, does this written statement accurately reflect your declaration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes, it reflects it completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And does this written statement accurately reflect what you would say if you were examined or questioned orally today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would seek to tender this particular statement under Rule 92 ter along with the associated exhibit, which now has the number P4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is admitted already into evidence, so tendering is not necessarily anymore, but a number has to be assigned to it; and then you said "with the associated exhibit," which is now P4. The exhibit would be -- the statement is 65 ter 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This last statement is 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you mean the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: P4, Your Honours, was the list of SMS messages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. And that's the only attachment you want to tender through this witness, or do we --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That was the only associated exhibit that we submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, there are -- I don't have to ask about objections. Mr. Registrar, would you please assign a number to 65 ter number P4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 4 becomes Exhibit Number P8, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P8 was admitted and is admitted under seal. Then the attached exhibit is already admitted as P4, Exhibit Number P4. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you explained to Witness 2 the procedure; that is, that the Chamber has read your statements and that you're here to answer questions by the Defence on the statement. Mr. Saxon, it's common in the Chambers I preside over that a very brief summary will be read into the record so that the public also knows what we are talking about. Perhaps you could do it at the beginning of tomorrow's session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dieckmann, is it again you who will first cross-examine the witness or is it Mr. Khan? Witness 2, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Dieckmann, who is counsel for Mr. Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness Number 2, my name is Jens Dieckmann, Defence counsel for Bajrush Morina, and I will ask you a couple of questions. I will try to ask my questions as short and clear as possible, and I would highly appreciate if you could try to answer also very briefly or clear if it's possible and proper for you. If you do not understand the question, please indicate it immediately to me that I ask you again. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes, okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, in the following, I put it to you that, first, Bajrush Morina did ask you during a telephone conversation on 2nd of July, 2007, when you were travelling to The Hague; secondly, I will put it to you that the intention of Bajrush Morina to meet with you was to get a confirmation from you that you stand behind the interview you'd given him in 2002; and, thirdly, that he did not influence you any way with regard to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, just a suggestion, that it might be more fair for the witness and perhaps better for the record if my learned colleague simply puts his questions one at a time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, Mr. Dieckmann was not putting questions yet to the witness. He was, from what I understand, he was fulfilling his obligation under Rule -- and I think it would be Rule 90(H) which says: "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." I think that's what Mr. Dieckmann did. At the same time, I would agree with Mr. Saxon that if you do that subject by subject, rather than the whole of your case, that might be easier for the witness to follow. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Witness, you know Bajrush Morina, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You met him personally first time in mid-July 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: No, that's not true -- yes, July 2002, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: At this time, you were in Pristina, Kosovo; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: But you only spent a short time in Pristina because at that time you lived in another country; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you already knew Bajrush Morina before your first meeting as a political journalist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes. He worked for the newspaper Bota Sot as head -- as editor-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. In summer 2002, you contacted the Bota Sot office to get in touch with Mr. Bajrush Morina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the editorial office for an interview, and he met me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: You finally met Bajrush Morina in his office as editor-in-chief in the Bota Sot office in Pristina; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: We met in one of the offices of the newspaper Bota Sot, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: And you met there in the morning time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was around noon time. I don't think it was in the morning, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. The interview you have had with Bajrush Morina, was it recorded, audio-recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes. I think Bajrush did record it or he took notes in his notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: This interview lasted about several hours, two, three hours, could you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: To your recollection, what was the interview about? Could you perhaps briefly summarize it, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 2
utterances.text: I'm not here to talk about that interview because it was published in Bota Sot; but, initially, he asked questions and I answered about events that had taken place during the war in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps, should we go in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That might be a wise thing to do. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. First of all, Witness 2, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone about the testimony, the testimony already given today or the testimony still to be given tomorrow, because we'll continue tomorrow. We adjourn and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 9th of September, at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of September, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.
